questions.stem: Pipe A fills a tank in 12 hours and Pipe B fills it in 8 hours. If both are opened together, how long to fill the tank?

options.option_text: 10 hours
4.8 hours
6 hours
3.6 hours

questions.explanation: Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/8 = 2/24 + 3/24 = 5/24 per hour. Time = 24/5 = 4.8 hours. LCM method: LCM(12,8)=24 units. A fills 2/hr, B fills 3/hr → 5/hr → 24/5 = 4.8 h.

questions.stem: A full tank has an inlet pipe that can fill it in 6 hours, and a drain pipe that can empty it in 4 hours. If both are opened when the tank is full, how long to empty the tank?

options.option_text: 4 hours
2.4 hours
12 hours
24 hours

questions.explanation: Net drain rate = 1/4 − 1/6 = 3/12 − 2/12 = 1/12 per hour (net emptying, since drain > fill). Time to empty full tank = 12 hours. Key: drain (1/4) > fill (1/6), so tank empties at net rate 1/12 per hour.

questions.stem: Pipes A (6 hr), B (9 hr), and C (12 hr) all fill a tank. All three opened together — how long to fill?

options.option_text: Exactly 3 hours at combined fill rate
Exactly 9 hours by averaging the three rates
Exactly 4 hours by simple addition method
Approx. 2.77 hours (36/13 hours)

questions.explanation: LCM(6,9,12) = 36. A=6 units/hr, B=4 units/hr, C=3 units/hr. Total = 13 units/hr. Time = 36/13 ≈ 2.77 hours. Alternatively: 1/6+1/9+1/12 = 6/36+4/36+3/36 = 13/36 → 36/13 h.

questions.stem: Pipes A (fills in 10 hr), B (fills in 15 hr), and C (drains in 20 hr) are all opened together. How long to fill the empty tank?

options.option_text: 60/7 hours (approx. 8.57 hours)
7.5 hours exactly with the three pipes
10 hours, same as the slowest filling pipe
6 hours with combined filling exceeding drain

questions.stem: A pipe fills a tank in 20 hours. Due to a leak in the bottom, the tank takes 60 hours to fill instead. How long will the leak alone take to empty a full tank?

options.option_text: 40 hours
20 hours
30 hours
12 hours

questions.explanation: With leak: net rate = 1/60. Pipe alone: 1/20. Leak rate = 1/20 − 1/60 = 3/60 − 1/60 = 2/60 = 1/30. So the leak alone empties the tank in 30 hours.

questions.stem: Pipe A fills a tank in 15 hr. Pipe B fills it in 10 hr. A is opened first. After 5 hours B is also opened. How many total hours to fill the tank?

options.option_text: 7.5 hours total from the start of the operation
9 hours total (5 hr A alone + 4 hr both together)
12 hours total including the initial solo filling
10 hours total, same as B alone filling the tank

questions.explanation: A alone for 5 hr fills 5/15 = 1/3. Remaining = 2/3. Combined rate = 1/15+1/10 = 2/30+3/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 per hour. Time to fill 2/3 at 1/6 per hour = (2/3)/(1/6) = 4 hours. Total = 5+4 = 9 hours.

questions.stem: Pipe A fills a tank in 12 hr, Pipe B in 18 hr. They alternate — A works 1st hour, B works 2nd hour, A works 3rd hour, and so on. How long to fill the empty tank?

options.option_text: 15 hours exactly at this alternating rate
14 hours exactly using the alternating method
16 hours due to the inefficiency of alternating pipes
14 hours 20 minutes (14⅓ hours)

questions.explanation: Per 2-hour cycle: 1/12+1/18 = 3/36+2/36 = 5/36. After 14 hours (7 complete cycles): 7×5/36 = 35/36 filled. Remaining = 1/36. In the 15th hour, A works at 1/12 = 3/36 per hour. Time to fill 1/36 at rate 3/36 = (1/36)/(3/36) = 1/3 hour = 20 minutes. Total = 14 hours 20 minutes.

questions.stem: A full cistern has two outlet pipes. Outlet P empties it in 10 hours and outlet Q empties it in 15 hours. Both outlets are opened simultaneously. In how many hours will the cistern be completely empty?

options.option_text: 4 hours — outlets combined as 1/4 per hour by direct addition
6 hours — combined drain rate 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 per hour
12 hours — arithmetic mean of the 10 and 15 hour drain times
30 hours — LCM of drain durations mistaken as the final answer

questions.explanation: Combined drain rate = 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 per hour. Time to empty = 6 hours. Option C (12 hours) is the arithmetic mean (10+15)/2 — a frequent error when students average times instead of adding rates. Option D (30 hours) confuses the LCM as the answer rather than using it as a computational tool to find the net rate.

questions.stem: A water tank is exactly three-quarters full. A drain pipe, which would empty a completely full tank in 12 hours, is opened. How long will it take to drain only the water currently present in the tank?

options.option_text: 8 hours — subtracting one-quarter of 12 hours from the full drain time
9 hours — draining 3/4 tank at rate 1/12 per hour gives exactly 9 hours
12 hours — full drain time applied without adjusting for partial volume
16 hours — inverting the fraction: 12 multiplied by 4/3 by mistake

questions.explanation: Work to drain = 3/4 of tank. Drain rate = 1/12 per hour. Time = (3/4) ÷ (1/12) = (3/4) × 12 = 9 hours. Option D (16 hours) is the classic inversion error: computing 12 ÷ (3/4) = 16 instead of multiplying. Option A (8 hours) wrongly subtracts (1/4 × 12 = 3) from 12 instead of scaling by the filled fraction.

questions.stem: Pipe A fills a cistern in 20 minutes and Pipe B fills it in 30 minutes. Both are opened simultaneously, but Pipe A is shut off after a while. The cistern is completely filled exactly 18 minutes after both pipes were first opened. For how many minutes was Pipe A kept open?

options.option_text: 6 minutes — one-third of 18 minutes allocated by simple proportion
8 minutes — A fills 2/5 of cistern at its 1/20 rate in exactly 8 min
10 minutes — A assumed to run until the halfway mark of total time
12 minutes — splitting 18 minutes equally between both pipes assumed

questions.explanation: Let A run for t minutes; B runs all 18 minutes. Equation: t/20 + 18/30 = 1 → t/20 + 3/5 = 1 → t/20 = 2/5 → t = 8 minutes. Option C (10 min) is tempting because A and B together would fill the tank in 12 minutes, so students assume A ran proportionally for 10 of 18 minutes — but this ignores that B alone covers the post-shutdown period.

questions.stem: A cistern is exactly one-third full. Pipe A, which fills the full cistern in 3 hours, and Pipe B, which drains the full cistern in 5 hours, are both opened simultaneously. How long will it take for the cistern to become completely full?

options.option_text: 2 hours — only Pipe A's rate applied to remaining 2/3 volume
5 hours — net fill rate 2/15 per hour covers the remaining 2/3 volume
2.5 hours — net rate 2/15 applied to the already-filled 1/3 portion
7.5 hours — net rate computed correctly but full empty tank assumed

questions.explanation: Net fill rate = 1/3 − 1/5 = 2/15 per hour. Remaining volume = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3. Time = (2/3) ÷ (2/15) = (2/3) × (15/2) = 5 hours. Option D (7.5 hours) is the most frequent error: the net rate 2/15 is derived correctly but applied to the full tank (15/2 = 7.5), forgetting 1/3 is already filled. Option C (2.5 hours) applies the net rate to the wrong portion — the filled 1/3 instead of the empty 2/3.

questions.stem: Pipe A fills a tank in 20 minutes, Pipe B fills it in 30 minutes, and Pipe C is a drain pipe. When all three pipes are opened together, the tank gets completely filled in 60 minutes. How long would Pipe C alone take to empty a full tank?

options.option_text: 12 minutes — C's drain rate wrongly set equal to A and B combined
15 minutes — C drains at rate 1/15 per minute, derived from net equation
20 minutes — C assumed to exactly offset only Pipe A's contribution
30 minutes — C assumed to exactly offset only Pipe B's contribution

questions.explanation: Combined fill rate of A and B = 1/20 + 1/30 = 5/60 = 1/12. With all three open, net fill rate = 1/60. So C's drain rate = 1/12 − 1/60 = 5/60 − 1/60 = 4/60 = 1/15. C alone empties in 15 minutes. Option A (12 minutes) is the classic trap: students set C equal to the A+B combined rate of 1/12, ignoring that the net 1/60 fill rate already accounts for C's drag on A+B.

questions.stem: A large inlet pipe fills a tank exactly 5 times faster than a small inlet pipe. Both were opened together, but the large pipe broke down after some time, and the small pipe alone then took 30 more minutes to complete the filling. The total fill time from start to finish was 50 minutes. In how many minutes can the large pipe alone fill the entire tank?

options.option_text: 25 minutes — derived from incorrectly estimating small pipe at 125 min
30 minutes — small pipe alone fills in 150 min, so large = 150 ÷ 5
35 minutes — obtained by averaging the breakdown instant and total time
40 minutes — computed from combined-work formula skipping breakdown step

questions.explanation: Large pipe broke at minute 50 − 30 = 20. Let small pipe alone take S minutes; large = S/5. Work equation: 20 × (5/S + 1/S) + 30 × (1/S) = 1 → 120/S + 30/S = 1 → S = 150. Large alone = 150/5 = 30 minutes. Option A (25 min) arises from an arithmetic slip where students read 150/S = 1 as S = 125 after mishandling the coefficient of the combined-work term.

questions.stem: Inlet pipes P and Q fill a cistern in 12 hours and 16 hours respectively. Outlet pipe R empties the full cistern in 8 hours. All three are opened simultaneously from empty. Due to scheduled power cuts, after every 2 hours of active operation the pipes stay closed for exactly 30 minutes. How many total hours (including all off-periods) does it take to completely fill the cistern?

options.option_text: 48 hours — net fill rate 1/48 applied directly, ignoring all off-periods
59 hours 30 minutes — 23 full 2.5-hour cycles then 2 final active hours
60 hours — 24 complete 2.5-hour cycles counted including last rest period
62 hours 30 minutes — one extra cycle added as buffer for uncertainty

questions.explanation: Net fill rate = 1/12 + 1/16 − 1/8 = 4/48 + 3/48 − 6/48 = 1/48 per hour. Each 2-hour active window fills 2/48 = 1/24 of tank. Each cycle = 2 hr active + 0.5 hr off = 2.5 hr. After 23 full cycles: 23/24 filled, 57.5 hours elapsed. Remaining 1/24 requires 2 more active hours (1/24 ÷ 1/48 = 2 exactly). Total = 57.5 + 2 = 59.5 hours = 59 hr 30 min. Option C (60 hours) is the common trap: students count 24 × 2.5 = 60, but the cistern fills at the end of the 24th active window — the subsequent 30-minute rest never begins.
